can a rival buy your brand name on amazon? kent ro has sued amazon in the delhi high court (cs(comm) 1145/2026). it alleges that its well-known mark "kent" is sold as an advertising keyword, so shoppers searching for kent purifiers see competing products first. 🔎 how keyword ads work a seller bids on "kent". a shopper searches "kent". a rival's product appears at the top, marked "sponsored". the platform earns on every click. the word "kent" may never appear in the ad, which courts call "invisible use". 📅 where the case stands • justice tejas karia issued summons on 16 october; amazon has accepted notice. • kent placed a video on record showing the keyword bidding process. • no interim relief yet. the application will be heard on 8 december. ⚖️ the law the court will apply 1️⃣ google v. drs logistics (division bench, 2023): using a mark as a keyword is "use" in advertising even if it's never shown, but it isn't infringement per se. there must be confusion, unfair advantage or dilution. google got no safe harbour because it actively promoted trademarks as keywords. 2️⃣ hindware v. grohe (may 2026): invisible keyword use is use; google "was not neutral but an active commercial participant". google has appealed. ❓ three questions for a marketplace • who is using the mark: the seller who bids, or the platform that runs the auction and earns from it? • is there confusion? the shopper is already inside the store and the ad says "sponsored", but kent is a well-known mark, which gets wider protection. • is amazon a passive intermediary? after drs and hindware, the search engine that sold keywords didn't get safe harbour. amazon will have to show its role is different. ✅ what this means now • brands: search your own name on marketplaces and keep a record of what appears. • sellers: bidding on a rival's well-known mark is a real litigation risk; personality rights aren't only for celebrities on 16 november, the madras high court restrained blinkit from using the persona of saravanan hari, the chennai super kings superfan, without his written consent. 📰 the facts • since around 2013, hari has appeared at csk matches with a yellow-painted face, curly wig, moustache, dhoni's no. 7 and a thumbs-up pose. it is widely covered on tv. • on 23 march 2025, a blinkit ad on the front page of the sunday times showed a cartoon figure with the same look and pose. • people he knew asked whether he was endorsing blinkit. pre-suit mediation failed, and he sued, claiming ₹1.1 crore. ⚖️ blinkit's defence: the characters were fictional and didn't resemble him. the court found a clear resemblance: the same pose was reproduced, and the public was likely to be misled into thinking it was him. 💬 the key line (justice p.b. balaji): "the constitution protects the rights of every individual and it need not be restricted or limited to celebrities like actors and sportspersons." blinkit could not exploit his personality rights, "whatever little it may be", for commercial gain without consent. 📌 relief (interim): no commercial use without written consent; the ad's artwork and emails must be preserved. the publisher's liability will be decided at trial. next hearing: 14 december. 🧭 where this fits in t. rangaraj (january 2026), the madras high court refused takedowns where posts merely circulated, insisting on commercial exploitation. hari's case applies the same test to a non-celebrity. read together, the test is identifiability plus commercial use without consent, not fame. 🔐 the privacy-law gap why not the dpdp act? section 3(c)(ii) excludes personal data that the person made publicly available, and a fan appearing on tv at matches may fall within that exclusion. most of the act also only applies from 13 may 2027. personality rights and passing off fill that gap. ✅ for brands and agencies 1️⃣ get written consent for any recognisable person, even as a cartoon or look-alike. 2️⃣ don't recreate a known pose or signature look. 3️⃣ ai-generated look-alikes carry the same risk. my take: if people recognise you, a brand needs your permission. that protects ordinary people without turning the right into a tool to silence fans, critics or the news. 📎 resources: • livelaw biz: https://www.livelawbiz.com/personality-rights/madras-high-court-protects-csk-fan-personality-rights-restraining-blinkit-from-using-image-without-consent-558695 • spicyip on t. rangaraj: https://spicyip.com/2026/01/a-course-correction-what-rangaraj-and-kamal-haasan-get-right-about-personality-rights.html should a local "famous face" have the same rights as a film star when a brand copies them? views are personal; hyderabad police now has an ai that maps "criminal networks". which law tells it where to stop? on 12 november, commissioner v.c. sajjanar launched dooradrishti, an ai platform built in-house by hyderabad city police. it compiles profiles of accused persons, analyses their activities and identifies links between individuals and criminal networks, using police databases and data from other departments. the stated aim: faster evidence, faster charge sheets, and a shift "from reactive to proactive policing". organised crime and cyber fraud do run through networks, so the aim is legitimate. but five questions haven't been answered publicly: 1️⃣ does it include people never convicted, or acquitted? 2️⃣ how does it make links, and how are false links caught? 3️⃣ does it reach beyond criminal records, to movements or activity? 4️⃣ who can access it, for how long, and is it audited? 5️⃣ must officers verify its findings before acting? the legal frame: 🔹 puttaswamy: state intrusion on privacy needs a law, a legitimate aim, proportionality and safeguards 🔹 dpdp act s. 17: processing to prevent, detect or investigate offences is largely exempt (from may 2027) 🔹 malak singh (1981): police surveillance registers must be limited to people reasonably suspected 🔹 criminal procedure (identification) act, 2022: records of people never convicted must be destroyed on release, discharge or acquittal and telangana has been here before. in 2022, the high court issued notice in s.q. masood's pil, india's first court challenge to police facial recognition without a law. the risk with network mapping is guilt by link: a relative, neighbour or client flagged by association, old firs and acquittals that never leave the system, and no way to know or correct your profile. being linked to someone isn't evidence of a crime. my take: six safeguards before scale (slide 7): ✔ a published legal basis and sop ✔ scope limited to charge-sheeted and convicted persons, for specific cases ✔ human verification: ai output is a lead, never evidence on its own ✔ deletion for the acquitted and discharged ✔ logs and independent audits of every search ✔ a right to know and correct one's profile, with an annual transparency report hyderabad can lead on ai policing. it should also lead on the rules. 📎 resources: • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d-ichntj • newsmeter: can a privacy law quietly weaken the right to information? the supreme court hears that question again on 17 november. last month i wrote about the news publishers' challenge to the dpdp act. but the larger case, venkatesh nayak v. union of india, goes well beyond journalism. rti activist venkatesh nayak, ncpri, the reporters' collective and nitin sethi filed in february. the court issued notice, refused an interim stay and referred the matter to a larger bench. the publishers' plea (dnpa) joined in october. the central challenge is s. 44(3), which rewrote rti s. 8(1)(j): 🔹 before: personal information was exempt only if unrelated to public activity or an unwarranted invasion of privacy, and could be disclosed if a larger public interest justified it 🔹 after: "information which relates mahajan dealt with a user whose instagram accounts were disabled without notice or specific reasons. the in-app review failed, and his appeal to the grievance appellate committee (gac) went undecided past its 30-day deadline. the court held: 🔹 a writ under article 226 isn't maintainable against meta. it doesn't perform a public function or discharge a public duty 🔹 instagram shapes public opinion, (order dated 26 october, reported 2 november), justices ajit kumar and garima prashad said "no private cctv camera can be installed and positioned in such a manner as to interfere with the privacy of a neighbour." the petitioner said his neighbour's camera covered his home's entrance and exit. the court didn't decide whether this camera crossed the line; it directed the district magistrate to decide his complaint within one month. other courts have drawn similar lines: 🔹 kerala hc (2023): security can't be a pretext to snoop on neighbours; the court asked the state police chief to frame cctv guidelines 🔹 calcutta hc, upheld by the supreme court (2025): cameras inside a shared house need the consent of all occupants 🔹 kerala hc (2025): a camera protecting an elderly woman facing real threats was allowed to stay so it's a balance. courts look at where the camera points, what it records, why it's there, and what's done with the footage. which law applies? a "digital arrest" victim sends the money themselves. until now, that meant the bank could say: not our problem. the supreme court has just changed that conversation. on 29 october, a bench of cji surya kant, justice joymalya bagchi and justice v. mohana, hearing the suo motu case on digital arrest scams, told the rbi that its new rules must include a liability clause: 🔹 banks must compensate victims where inadequate safeguards or a failure of due diligence contributed to the fraud 🔹 compensation of not less than the amount the customer lost 🔹 the bank pays, not just the employee involved ("the bank will have to pay," said the cji) 🔹 safeguards to consider: temporarily holding transactions out of line with an account's history, automatic alerts to police, and verification before release why this matters: the rbi's 2017 circular gives zero liability for "unauthorised" transactions where the bank is at fault. but in a digital arrest, the victim authorises the transfer, under fear and deception. so victims have often fallen outside it, even when the bank let sudden, unusual transfers through without a single check. what's next: the rbi has proposed notifying its kyc amendment directions by 30 november (also the next hearing) and bringing them into force by 31 december. separately, a draft would let banks flag and hold suspected mule-account transactions, and the government has proposed a one-hour delay on payments of ₹10,000 or more. my take: five questions the final rules must answer. 1️⃣ who decides that due diligence failed? not the bank alone; the burden should stay on the bank, as in 2017 2️⃣ what counts as due diligence? clear triggers: large first-time transfers, new payees, elderly or dormant accounts 3️⃣ how fast is the refund? a provisional credit within days, not years of litigation 4️⃣ who is covered? nbfcs, wallets and payment apps too 5️⃣ what about genuine payments? holds need short time limits and a quick release route if you get the call: no indian agency arrests anyone over a video call, and no genuine officer asks you to transfer money to "verify" it. if you've already paid, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in immediately, tell your bank in writing, file an fir, and escalate to the rbi ombudsman if needed (slide 7). please share this with your parents and grandparents. they're the most frequent targets. 📎 resources: • business standard: https://lnkd.in/dcvh2qjq • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d7btemea • report cyber fraud: https://cybercrime.gov.in should banks bear the loss when their systems miss an obvious red flag? a creator's posts were taken down over copyright complaints. then his whole instagram account was suspended. no notice, no hearing. the high court says that's within the rules. in anmol jain v. union of india (order dated 17 september, reported 27 october), the madhya pradesh high court dismissed a meme creator's challenge to rule 3(1)(b)(iv) of the it rules, 2021. his page had about 39,000 followers and was a source of income. he argued that a private company shouldn't decide copyright infringement; only courts should. the court held: 🔹 instagram is an intermediary under s. 2(w) of the it act, with due-diligence duties that include acting against infringing content 🔹 once the law lets a private company operate as an intermediary, it may manage and control its platform 🔹 the grievance officer (rule 3(2)) and the grievance appellate committee (rule 3a) are adequate safeguards what it means for creators, in order: 1️⃣ appeal in-app straight away 2️⃣ grievance officer: must acknowledge in 24 hours and resolve in 15 days 3️⃣ grievance appellate committee: appeal online at gac.gov.in within 30 days 4️⃣ then other legal routes, including action against a bad-faith claimant the gap: the copyright rules, 2013 (rule 75) build in a check. the complainant must identify the work and its ownership, and if no court order follows within 21 days, the content may be restored. in practice, platform policy decides, at scale, and creators often never see the complaint. memes and reviews may be fair dealing under s. 52(1)(a), but a platform team makes that call, not a judge. my take: the court is right that platforms must act on infringement. but the process needs: ✔ notice to the creator: the complaint, the claimant and the work said to be copied ✔ proportionality: remove the post first; suspend accounts only for repeat infringement, after warnings ✔ checks on false claims used to silence rivals or critics ✔ published gac decisions, and platform compliance with them checklist for creators and brands (slide 7): use licensed music and clips, keep licences and original files, screenshot every notice, track the 30-day gac deadline, record lost income, and back up your content. on someone else's platform, your rights are mostly procedural. use every step. 📎 resources: • livelaw on the ruling: https://lnkd.in/dkndvagy • lawbeat on the ruling: can a privacy law stop journalists from doing their job? india's biggest media houses have asked the supreme court. reuters reported on 26 october that 21 news publishers, acting through the digital news publishers association (dnpa), have challenged the digital personal data protection act. dnpa members include network18, ndtv, the indian express and times internet. the case is listed for hearing on 27 october. they want key provisions struck down before they take effect in may 2027. their four concerns: 🔹 notice and consent (ss. 5–6): journalists may need consent from the very people they investigate 🔹 erasure (ss. 8(7), 12): withdrawal of consent and erasure with no public-interest safeguard could force stories off the record 🔹 information demands (s. 36 with rule 23): the centre can call for information from any data fiduciary, risking exposure of sources 🔹 blocking (s. 37): access can be blocked "in the interests of the general public" underneath it all: there is no exemption for journalism. the 2018 draft, the 2019 bill and the 2021 jpc version all had one. it was dropped in 2022. the state gets wide exemptions under s. 17; the press gets none. the government's position: in july 2025, meity told media bodies no exemption was needed, said journalists aren't data fiduciaries, and offered faqs. separate petitions by venkatesh nayak, the reporters' collective and ncpri (on the rti amendment and s. 36) were referred to a larger bench in february 2026, without a stay. today, a journalist's only clear relief is s. 3(c)(ii): data the person (or a legal duty) made public falls outside the act. most investigative material doesn't fit. my take: fix it, don't scrap it. 1️⃣ put the exemption in the law; an faq can't override the text 2️⃣ base it on purpose (journalism in the public interest), not status, so freelancers are covered 3️⃣ keep security and breach duties; newsrooms hold sensitive data too 4️⃣ require independent or judicial approval before s. 36 demands reach journalistic material 5️⃣ apply a public-interest test before published reports or archives are erased the eu, uk and singapore all build this balance in (slide 5). newsroom can an ai company train on indian news without permission? in ani media pvt. ltd. v. open ai opco llc, cs(comm) 1028/2024, the delhi high court has given india its first answer, at least for now. on 24 july 2026, justice amit bansal dismissed ani's application for an interim injunction (i.a. 45300/2024). the key takeaways: 1️⃣ jurisdiction (paras 48–55): storing ani's works on us servers is only the "terminal step in the chain of events" that begins with accessing them from india. moving servers abroad cannot be used to evade indian copyright law. 2️⃣ storage is reproduction (paras 145–151): under section 14(a)(i), storing a work "in any medium by electronic means", temporarily or permanently, is reproduction. but section 14 operates "subject to the provisions of this act", so an act covered by section 52 is not infringement. 3️⃣ fair dealing under section 52(1)(a)(i) (paras 190–255): • commercial use alone does not exclude the defence (para 190) • "private" is not limited to individuals and can cover a company using data in a closed space (paras 208–211) • "research" gets an updating construction and extends to machine learning (para 218) • instead of the us four-factor test, the court applied a purpose test and a fairness test: no market substitution of ani's news feed was shown, and the public interest in llms was established (paras 234–255) 4️⃣ outputs (para 271): chatgpt's outputs, including those generated using rag, were prima facie not substantially similar to ani's works, and ani failed to show memorisation or regurgitation. the 14 articles relied on were published after the models' training cut-offs. 5️⃣ balance of convenience (paras 262–270): ani had not used the available opt-out to block openai's crawlers, and an injunction would harm the public at large. what it leaves open: • will this broad reading of "private use, including research" survive appeal or the final hearing? the court itself notes its observations have no bearing on the outcome of the suit (para 274). • how does it sit alongside gema v. openai in germany and thomson reuters v. ross in the us third circuit, which went the other way on their facts?
